title: Cell Membrane
summary: The cell membrane is the flexible outer boundary of every cell — a thin double layer that decides what enters and what leaves. Explore its structure of lipids and proteins and its selective semi-permeable action, then see why everything a cell takes in or releases must cross this controlled barrier.

compareCandidate.label: Cell membrane vs. cell wall
compareCandidate.description: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible, living layer present in ALL cells that controls what enters and exits. The cell wall is a thick, rigid, non-living coating found outside the membrane only in plants, fungi, and some bacteria, which gives the cell support and shape.

processes: Selective — semi-permeable — transport of water and small molecules
Diffusion and osmosis across the bilayer

plainLanguageExplanation: The cell membrane is the skin of the cell — a very thin, flexible wrapping that holds the cell together and separates its insides from the outside world. It is built from a double layer of oily molecules (lipids), called a bilayer, with many proteins floating within it, and it acts as a selective security gate. Not everything passes through equally: small, simple molecules like water and oxygen slip through easily, nutrients the cell needs are let in through special proteins, and waste or harmful things are kept out or moved out. This pick-and-choose control is called selective permeability, and because the membrane let some things through but not others, it is the reason a cell can keep a stable, healthy inside even when the outside changes.

keyFacts.label: Where it is
keyFacts.value: The thin outer boundary of every cell, separating the cytoplasm from the outside

keyFacts.label: Made of
keyFacts.value: A double layer of phospholipids with proteins and other molecules embedded in it

keyFacts.label: Main job
keyFacts.value: Controls what enters and leaves: a selective, semi-permeable barrier

keyFacts.label: Flexibility
keyFacts.value: It is flexible and can bend and move, allowing cells to change shape

keyFacts.label: In all cells
keyFacts.value: Every cell has a membrane - even bacteria (in addition to a wall in plant cells)

keyFacts.label: Selective part
keyFacts.value: Small molecules like water pass through freely; larger or charged ones need protein doors

whyItMatters: The cell membrane is what makes a cell a cell — a separate, living unit with control over its own internal conditions. Keeping the right ingredients inside and the wrong ones out is the very definition of being alive at the cellular level. Understanding it unlocks big things you rely on: how cells get nutrients, how cells communicate, how medicines deliver their effects, and how a single cell can keep a stable 'inside' no matter what happens 'outside.'
tagline: The selective gateway of the cell
didYouKnow: Your body is made of trillions of cells, each wrapped in its own membrane that decides, second by second, which molecules are allowed through the gate.
